title: Building Sub-2s AI Voice Pipelines with Flask
excerpt: How I optimized real-time voice processing to achieve production-grade latency for multilingual AI conversations...

content.text: When I joined Salescode.ai, one of my first challenges was building a real-time voice calling agent that could hold natural conversations in multiple languages. The target? Sub-2-second end-to-end latency. Here's how we achieved it.
The Challenge

Voice AI pipelines involve multiple sequential steps: capturing audio, converting speech to text (STT), processing the intent, generating a response, and converting it back to speech (TTS). Each step adds latency, and users expect near-instant responses in a conversation.
Our requirements were demanding:

items: Support Hindi and Mexican Spanish with 90%+ accuracy
End-to-end latency under 2 seconds
Handle concurrent calls without degradation
Graceful fallback when AI confidence is low

content.text: Architecture Decisions

We chose Flask for our microservices because of its lightweight nature and Python's rich ecosystem for AI/ML integrations. The key architectural decision was using an async pipeline with streaming wherever possible.
Optimization Strategies
The biggest wins came from three key optimizations:
1. Streaming STT
Instead of waiting for the complete audio to finish before starting transcription, we streamed audio chunks to the STT service. This alone saved 300-500ms on average.
2. Response Pre-computation

We started generating AI responses as soon as we had 80% confidence in the transcription, rather than waiting for the final result. If the transcription changed significantly, we'd regenerate — but in 90% of cases, the early prediction was accurate enough.
3. Connection Pooling

External API calls (AWS Transcribe, 11 Labs TTS) were the biggest bottleneck. We implemented connection pooling and keep-alive connections, reducing the overhead of each API call from ~200ms to ~50ms.

# Connection pool for external services
from urllib3 import PoolManager

pool = PoolManager(
    num_pools=10,
    maxsize=20,
    retries=3,
    timeout=Timeout(connect=1.0, read=3.0)
)

# Reuse connections across requests
tts_client = TTSClient(http_pool=pool)
stt_client = STTClient(http_pool=pool)
Results
After these optimizations, our pipeline consistently delivered:

items: **Average latency:** 1.4 seconds (down from 3.2s)
**P95 latency:** 1.8 seconds
**Accuracy:** 90-95% across Hindi and Mexican Spanish
**Concurrent calls:** 50+ without degradation

content.text: Key Takeaways

Building real-time AI systems taught me that the biggest performance gains come from architectural decisions, not micro-optimizations. Streaming, early prediction, and connection reuse were far more impactful than tweaking individual function performance.
If you're building similar systems, start by profiling your entire pipeline end-to-end. The bottleneck is almost never where you think it is.

title: Docker + AWS: My Production Deployment Playbook
excerpt: A practical guide to deploying Python microservices on AWS EC2 with Docker, Nginx, and zero-downtime updates...

content.text: When I first started deploying Python microservices for our AI voice products, the sheer number of architectural choices on AWS was overwhelming. ECS, EKS, Lambda—each has its place, but when you need direct control, low latency for persistent socket connections, and predictable costs, a solid EC2 + Docker + Nginx setup remains a battle-tested approach.
Here is the playbook I use to deploy our production-grade Python (Flask) microservices, ensuring zero-downtime updates and reliable scaling.
1. Containerizing the Python Microservice

The foundation of a reliable deployment is a reproducible artifact. I always rely on multi-stage Docker builds to keep the final image lightweight and secure. By separating the build environment from the runtime environment, we reduce the attack surface and speed up CI/CD pipelines.

# Build Stage
FROM python:3.10-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt

# Runtime Stage
FROM python:3.10-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
CMD ["gunicorn", "-w", "4", "-k", "uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker", "-b", "0.0.0.0:8000", "app:app"]
2. Nginx as the Gatekeeper
Instead of exposing the Docker container directly to the web, Nginx acts as a reverse proxy on the EC2 instance. This provides several benefits:

items: **SSL Termination:** Offloading HTTPS processing so the Python app can focus solely on business logic.
**Load Balancing:** Seamlessly routing traffic between multiple containers.
**Static File Caching:** Serving assets directly without hitting the application server.

content.text: 3. CI/CD Integration with Jenkins
To eliminate manual regression and deployment errors, I integrated our Playwright and Flutter automation suites directly into a Jenkins CI/CD pipeline.

items: **Lint & Test:** Every pull request triggers unit tests and API validations across our 500+ data points.
**Build & Push:** On merge, Jenkins builds the new Docker image and pushes it to an internal registry.
**Deploy:** The pipeline SSHs into the EC2 instance, pulls the latest image, and gracefully restarts the containers.

content.text: 4. Live Issue Resolution
In production, things break. My go-to tools for live debugging on EC2 include:

items: `docker stats` for real-time CPU and memory monitoring.
`docker logs -f --tail 100 <container_id>` to trace backend errors immediately.
CloudWatch alarms set up for high memory utilization, ensuring we can intervene before an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) kill occurs.

content.text: Helpful Resources

items: [Docker Multi-stage Builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/)
[Deploying Nginx Reverse Proxy](https://docs.nginx.com/nginx/admin-guide/web-server/reverse-proxy/)
[AWS EC2 Best Practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-best-practices.html)

title: STT vs TTS: Lessons from Building Conversational AI
excerpt: What I learned integrating speech-to-text and text-to-speech services across AWS, Google, and 11 Labs APIs...

content.text: Building an AI voice calling agent that feels naturally conversational is one of the hardest engineering challenges I've tackled. At Salescode.ai, achieving a sub-2-second response latency while maintaining ~90-95% accuracy in languages like Hindi and Mexican Spanish required a deep dive into the inner workings of Speech-to-Text (STT) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) pipelines.
Here are the critical lessons I learned optimizing our real-time AI workflows.
1. The Latency Bottleneck: Sequential vs. Streaming
A traditional sequential pipeline (Wait for user to stop talking -> STT -> LLM -> TTS) is far too slow for human conversation, often resulting in 3-4 seconds of awkward silence.
The breakthrough came from shifting to a streaming architecture:

items: **Partial ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition):** Instead of waiting for the user to finish speaking completely, we stream audio chunks via WebSockets to our STT provider (Google Cloud/AWS). We capture *partial* transcripts and feed them to the LLM as early context.

**Chunked TTS:** Once the LLM generates the first few tokens, we immediately send them to the TTS engine (like 11 Labs). We synthesize and stream the audio back to the user phrase-by-phrase, reducing the "Time to First Audio" (TTFA) to well under a second.

content.text: 2. Overcoming STT Accuracy Challenges
Handling regional accents (especially mixed-language scenarios like "Hinglish") is notoriously difficult. We found that relying on a single provider wasn't enough.

items: **Custom Vocabulary:** We heavily utilized AWS Transcribe's custom vocabulary features to teach the engine domain-specific sales terminology.

**Noise Filtering:** Implementing aggressive background noise suppression before the audio hits the STT engine drastically improved our transcription accuracy, keeping it consistently in the 90-95% range.

content.text: 3. The Nuance of TTS Generation
For TTS, creating a voice that doesn't sound robotic is key to user retention. While services like 11 Labs provide incredibly realistic voices, their API calls can be latency-heavy.

items: **Caching Common Responses:** For frequent conversational fillers (e.g., "Got it," "Let me check on that," "Mhm"), we pre-synthesize and cache the audio files. This allows the system to respond instantly while the heavier LLM processing happens in the background.

content.text: Building production-grade AI pipelines requires treating latency as a feature, not just a metric. By obsessively optimizing the handoffs between STT, LLM, and TTS, we were able to create a seamless, human-like voice experience.

items: [Google Cloud Speech-to-Text Streaming API](https://cloud.google.com/speech-to-text/docs/streaming-recognize)
[AWS Transcribe Custom Vocabularies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transcribe/latest/dg/custom-vocabulary.html)
[ElevenLabs API Documentation](https://elevenlabs.io/docs/api-reference/text-to-speech)
